strengths: Systematic and well-designed benchmark (VLMBias) with 7 diverse task categories spanning animals, logos, flags, chess, games, optical illusions, and patterns
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 7 state-of-the-art VLMs including reasoning models (o4-mini, o3)
Clear presentation with intuitive visualizations of VLM failure modes
Strong reproducibility: extensive appendices with detailed prompts, implementation pipelines, ground truth calculations, and promised code/data release
Important research question about whether VLMs perform actual visual reasoning vs. rely on memorized prior knowledge
Well-engineered automated pipeline for generating counter-factual images and systematic evaluation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core finding that VLMs are biased and rely on prior knowledge is already established in prior work [32, 28]; this paper validates but does not provide fundamental new insights

Critical absence of human baselines: without human performance on identical modified images, impossible to determine if VLM failures are abnormally poor or reflect genuine task difficulty; severely limits interpretability
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: documents THAT biases exist but barely explores WHY; lacks attention visualizations, component-level ablations, or evidence for the 'memorized knowledge' hypothesis

Weak proposed solutions: simple prompts improve accuracy by only +1.87-+2.70 points; limited exploration of sophisticated prompting strategies (chain-of-thought); conclusion that 'helpful prompts don't work' may be premature
Questionable task design for some domains: optical illusions test on artificial 'reversed' versions unrepresentative of real scenarios; patterned grid connection to practical bias is tenuous
No comparison to alternative baselines: lacks comparison to simpler vision models (CLIP) or prior VLM bias benchmarks (HallusionBench, VisualHallucination); difficult to assess relative contribution

Artificial evaluation scope: all tasks involve generated/modified images with systematic alterations; unclear whether findings generalize to real-world VLM applications (image captioning, visual QA) with organic images
No ablation on modification magnitude: single-run results without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; reliability unclear
Missing human comparison prevents assessing whether modified images are genuinely difficult or VLMs fail specifically due to bias

Ground truth definitions sometimes subjective: what VLMs 'should' answer based on prior knowledge is not always clearly justified; confounding factors (resolution, clarity) not disentangled from genuine bias

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark spanning 7 diverse tasks with ~1,400 high-quality images across multiple domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, games, optical illusions, patterned grids)
Clear, dramatic, and consistent findings across 5 state-of-the-art VLMs: 100% accuracy on originals drops to ~17% on modified counterfactual images
Thorough experimental methodology with automated image generation pipelines, systematic variations, multiple image resolutions, and human quality control
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive appendices with complete implementation details, all prompts and ground truth calculations documented, promised code/data release
Practical value for community: benchmark will be useful for evaluating VLM robustness and comparing approaches
Well-structured and clearly presented with compelling visual examples demonstrating specific VLM failure modes
Findings are consistent and reinforcing across multiple domains, question types, and models, suggesting systematic bias rather than isolated failures
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core observation that VLMs rely on memorized knowledge rather than visual analysis is not new; recent literature has documented VLM hallucinations and visual reasoning failures

Shallow root cause analysis: paper identifies WHAT the biases are but provides limited insight into WHY; no investigation of which components (vision encoder vs. language model) are responsible; no comparison with baseline approaches
Limited exploration of solutions: only tests two prompting strategies with minimal improvements (~2 points); no investigation of fine-tuning, architectural changes, or other mitigation approaches

Benchmark design limitations: tasks are somewhat artificial and carefully constructed, modifications are relatively obvious in some cases, limited to well-known subjects, and question types are relatively simple (counting, Y/N)
Lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; only 5 models tested; single-shot evaluation with no multiple runs reported

Evaluation concerns: ground truth for optical illusions relies on subjective human perception; some counting questions potentially ambiguous; no inter-rater reliability reported; limited discussion of annotation errors
Unclear generalization: scope limited to specific tasks and well-known subjects; generalization to smaller/open-source models, real-world scenarios, or non-English prompts is uncertain
Incomplete practical guidance: limited discussion of implications for real-world VLM deployment, which applications are most vulnerable, or how practitioners should handle these limitations
Presentation: at 52 pages with extensive appendices, paper could be more concise; some figures are small and difficult to read; occasional redundancy between main paper and appendix

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark (VLMBias) with 1,392 counterfeitual images across 7 diverse domains and systematic modifications
Thorough empirical evaluation with multiple ablations, sanity checks, background removal experiments, and human baselines
Clear presentation of failure modes with effective visualizations and systematic documentation across multiple VLMs
Actionable diagnostic insight that background removal significantly improves performance (from 17% to ~40%)
Well-controlled experiments with repeated runs and cross-domain validation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core insight that VLMs rely on prior knowledge over visual information is well-established in existing literature on VLM hallucinations and biases
No meaningful solutions proposed: Paper is purely diagnostic without proposing architectural changes, training methods, or practical remedies beyond background removal (which is often impractical)
Artificial and limited task scope: Simple counting/identification tasks with unclear relevance to real-world VLM applications
Shallow mechanistic analysis: Shows THAT biases exist but not WHY; lacks investigation of attention patterns, internal representations, or decision-making processes
Statistical rigor concerns: Most results lack confidence intervals or significance tests despite extensive testing; human study has small sample size (n=78)
Image generation bias: Acknowledged limitation that modifications are generated with specific tools (Gemini, GPT-4o) which may introduce their own biases
Limited practical impact: Does not provide actionable guidance for practitioners, users, or researchers on how to address identified biases
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Limited comparison with specialized models and missing ablations on model components that contribute to bias

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark (VLMBias) with 1,392 counteractual images across 7 diverse domains, systematically created with rigorous quality control
Thorough experimental evaluation spanning 5 SOTA VLMs with multiple ablations (background removal, reasoning tokens, few-shot learning, tool access) that systematically characterize failure modes
Rigorous methodology including sanity checks, human study validation with 78 participants reaching 96.88% accuracy, and multiple resolution testing
Clear, quantified findings with important practical implications (e.g., 75.70% bias rate on counteractual images, +21.09 accuracy gain from background removal)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices documenting task design, prompts, data generation pipelines, and promised code/data release
Significant practical relevance for understanding VLM limitations and implications for safety-critical deployments
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations and logical flow from problem identification through systematic characterization
weaknesses: Core finding that VLMs rely on prior knowledge over visual evidence is somewhat expected and builds incrementally on prior bias literature rather than presenting novel insights
Limited mechanistic analysis of why failures occur; paper is primarily empirical documentation of failures rather than investigation of underlying causes in vision encoders or reasoning stages
Minimal exploration of mitigation strategies; while problems are well-characterized, concrete solutions or guidance for model improvement are largely absent
Narrow evaluation scope: only 5 VLMs tested; missing comparisons with non-VLM baselines or models specialized for counting/visual reasoning tasks
Statistical rigor could be improved: limited confidence intervals, significance testing, or prediction uncertainty estimates provided; variation across runs noted but not fully quantified
Human study is modest in scale (78 participants) and uses somewhat artificial time-pressure conditions (0.2-2s exposure); limited exploration of alternative evaluation protocols
Paper density and length (73 pages) with substantial appendices makes the contribution somewhat difficult to synthesize; some redundancy could be condensed
